passage:
Joseph's broken leg was in its fifth week, the hostel lift had been broken for three days, and his roommate Jatin was away for exams. Joseph lived on the third floor.
On Monday, fed up, he tried the stairs without crutches, just to prove he could. He made it one flight before the pain forced him to sit, sweating, on the landing. On Tuesday he gave up altogether: he skipped his exercises, lay in bed and ignored his phone.
On Wednesday Jatin called. "You sound terrible."
"I'm useless. I can't even get down for food."
"You're not useless. You're healing. What did the physio say?"
"Small exercises every day. Crutches on stairs."
"Then do that. I'll ask the mess to send dinner up till I'm back."
That evening Joseph did his exercises, slowly, then crossed off the day on his calendar.

qa.q: Which floor did Joseph live on?
qa.a: Joseph lived on the third floor.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and useless, so he gave up, skipped his exercises and ignored his phone.

qa.q: What approach helped Joseph more than overdoing or giving up?
qa.a: Doing the physio's small exercises each day and using crutches on stairs, a steady pace instead of either extreme.

qa.q: What was Wednesday's call like for Jatin?
qa.a: Jatin was worried, hearing Joseph sound terrible, and wanted to help from a distance.

grounding: It shows a young adult frustrated by slow healing and dependence, swinging between overdoing and giving up, before settling on steady progress.

passage:
Kashish could not tie her own hair. Her shoulder was strapped after the scooter fall, and every morning in their Mumbai flat, her sister Sabina had to plait it for her.
"Pull harder, it's messy," Kashish snapped.
"I'm doing my best."
That afternoon, alone, Kashish tried to lift a full bucket to prove she was fine. Pain shot down her arm and she sat on the bathroom floor. By evening she refused to do her stretches at all. "What's the point? It'll never get better."
Sabina sat beside her. "It is getting better. Last week you couldn't lift a cup."
Kashish looked at her hand.
"Let's write down one small thing each day," Sabina said. "Stretches, then one new thing."
The next day Kashish wrote: Buttoned my own kurta. She showed Sabina, grinning.

qa.q: What did Kashish write down the next day?
qa.a: She wrote: Buttoned my own kurta.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel about needing Sabina to plait her hair?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and dependent, which is why she snapped at Sabina.

qa.q: What did Sabina suggest instead of overdoing or giving up?
qa.a: Writing down one small thing each day, doing the stretches and then one new task, so progress stays steady and visible.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel when Kashish snaps at her?
qa.a: Sabina may feel hurt but understands the frustration, and still helps with patience.

grounding: It shows a young adult impatient and dependent during recovery, swinging between overdoing and giving up, and a sibling encouraging steady progress.

passage:
Thursday
Six weeks since the accident and I'm still on crutches. I hate it. Bidisha has to carry my plate, open doors, help me with my socks. I'm twenty and I feel like a child. On Monday I was so fed up I walked to the end of the lane without crutches to prove something. My leg swelled up like a balloon and I spent two days in bed, sulking and refusing the exercises. Today the physio sat me down. 'You're doing all or nothing. Neither works.' She wrote a plan: ten minutes of exercises morning and evening, walking a little further each week. It sounds so slow I want to scream. But Bidisha drew a chart on the fridge, and I ticked the first box tonight.
Nitin

qa.q: What did Bidisha draw on the fridge?
qa.a: A chart.

qa.q: How does Nitin feel about needing help from Bidisha?
qa.a: Nitin feels frustrated and dependent, like a child, and hates it.

qa.q: What went wrong on Monday, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Nitin overdid it and then gave up for two days; a steady daily plan with small weekly steps can fix it.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel helping Nitin every day?
qa.a: Bidisha may feel tired and a bit worried, but glad to help with the chart.

grounding: Shows a young adult frustrated by slow healing and dependence, swinging between overdoing and giving up, and learning that steady progress works better.

passage:
Tenzin: my wrist is useless. 5 weeks after surgery and I still can't write properly
Mahima: that's so frustrating
Tenzin: yesterday I did double the physio to speed it up. today it's so sore I've done nothing at all
Mahima: ah, the all-or-nothing thing again
Tenzin: I hate needing my roommate to cut my food. I'm 21!
Mahima: I know. but what did the physio actually say?
Tenzin: 3 short sessions a day. every day. no extra
Mahima: so what if you just do that? even on sore days, the gentle version?
Tenzin: boring
Mahima: boring works. remember my ankle last year?
Tenzin: ok. 3 sessions. setting reminders now
Mahima: and text me a tick after each one. I'll cheer

qa.q: How many weeks after surgery is Tenzin?
qa.a: Five weeks.

qa.q: How is Tenzin feeling about the slow recovery?
qa.a: Tenzin feels frustrated and impatient, and embarrassed about depending on the roommate.

qa.q: What does Mahima encourage instead of all-or-nothing?
qa.a: Doing the three short physio sessions every day as advised, with a gentle version on sore days.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel cheering Tenzin on?
qa.a: Mahima probably feels caring and supportive, remembering a similar recovery.

grounding: Shows a young adult impatient and dependent during a slow recovery, swinging between overdoing and giving up, and learning that steady measured progress works better.

passage: After the scooter fall, Parul, twenty, came home to her village near Sangli to recover. Her leg was in a brace, and she could barely reach the well. Her mother had to help her bathe, and the neighbours visited to stare. Parul felt useless and cross all the time. One morning she tried to carry a bucket to prove she could, and fell. The next week she refused to do any exercises at all. Irfan, who helped at the village physio clinic, came by on his cycle. 'You're doing too much, then nothing. The bone doesn't like either.' He showed her three simple exercises. 'Every morning. Then walk to the temple steps and back. Next week, to the peepal tree.' Parul grumbled. By the end of the month she reached the peepal tree, and she laughed at herself for arguing.

qa.q: How far did Parul reach by the end of the month?
qa.a: The peepal tree.

qa.q: How was Parul feeling during her recovery?
qa.a: She felt useless, cross and impatient, dependent on her mother.

qa.q: What did Irfan suggest to replace doing too much and then nothing?
qa.a: Three simple exercises every morning and a walking distance that grows a little each week.

qa.q: How might Parul's mother have felt when Parul fell carrying the bucket?
qa.a: Her mother was probably frightened and worried, and relieved when Parul began steady exercises.

grounding: Shows a young adult frustrated by slow healing and dependence, swinging between overdoing and giving up, and finding that steady measured progress works better.

passage: Six weeks after the cycling accident, Daniel still needed Zeynep to carry his coffee from the kitchen of their Hamburg flat. "I can do it," he snapped, and tried, and the mug slid off the crutch handle onto the floor. On Monday he had done double his physio exercises, sure it would speed things up, and spent Tuesday unable to bend his knee. On Wednesday he refused to do any at all and stayed in bed scrolling. "This is taking forever," he told Zeynep. She handed him the chart from the physio. "You said the same last week. Look, you're bending further than in March." Daniel looked at the numbers. Grudgingly, he set a timer for the ten-minute routine, just the amount the physio had set, and did it.

qa.q: What happened when Daniel tried to carry his own coffee?
qa.a: The mug slid off the crutch handle onto the floor.

qa.q: How was Daniel feeling about his recovery, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was impatient and annoyed, snapping at Zeynep and saying it was taking forever.

qa.q: What went wrong on Monday and Wednesday, and what works better?
qa.a: He overdid the exercises, then gave up entirely; doing the set routine steadily each day works better than either extreme.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeynep to help Daniel through this?
qa.a: It is probably tiring and a bit hurtful when he snaps, but she stays patient and points to his real progress.

grounding: Shows a young adult in recovery impatient and dependent, swinging between overdoing and giving up, and steady measured progress as the better path.
